statement: A bakery sells rolls at 3 euros each, in bags of 4 for 10 euros, or in boxes of 10 for 22 euros. Sam needs at least 17 rolls. What is the least amount he can pay?

choices.misconception: I worked out the box price per roll, 2.20 euros, and multiplied by 17, as if the shop sold any number at that price.
I bought a box and two bags to get 18 rolls without checking whether 3 single rolls would be cheaper than the second bag.
I bought four bags and one single roll and never tried using a box.
I bought all 17 rolls one at a time at 3 euros each.

hints: Start with the cheapest way to buy most of the rolls.
A box is the cheapest price per roll, then a bag, then single rolls. Take one box and work out the cheapest way to get the remaining rolls, then compare with plans that use no box or two boxes.
One box gives 10 rolls for 22 euros. For the other 7: a bag and 3 singles cost 10 + 9 = 19 euros, while two bags cost 20 euros and seven singles cost 21 euros.

solutions.reliable: Compare the plans in steps. Per roll, a box costs 2.20 euros, a bag 2.50 euros and a single 3 euros, so buy a box first: 10 rolls for 22 euros. Sam still needs 7 rolls. Two bags (8 rolls) cost 20 euros, one bag and 3 singles cost 10 + 9 = 19 euros, and 7 singles cost 21 euros, so the best is 19 euros, a total of 22 + 19 = 41 euros. Other plans are dearer: two boxes cost 44 euros, and without a box the best is four bags and a single for 43 euros. The least he can pay is 41 euros. The transferable idea: in a multi-step money problem, settle the big cheap block first, then compare every option for the leftover rather than assuming the next bulk deal is best.

whyOnTest: Multi-step shopping problems test whether you compare every option for the leftover instead of grabbing the next bulk deal.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
